title: Kedoshim: the corners of the field (Leviticus 19:9–10)
hook: leave the field's edges and fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kedoshim opened with a call to everyone. Your line was holiness for everyone. Which ordinary thing did you do carefully? Today, the first of those ordinary places: a field at harvest. Day four hundred eleven.

A field of barley at harvest, gold to the edges. The owner planted it, waited on the rain, and counts every stalk as his. The harvesters are swinging their sickles toward the far end. In the Book of Ruth, a young widow from Moab, poor and far from home, walks into a field like this one, behind the harvesters, and starts picking up what they drop. Nobody chases her off. Because the owner of the field had been told, long before, to leave her something.
screen: `GOLD TO THE EDGES.` → `A WIDOW BEHIND THE HARVESTERS.` → `NOBODY CHASES HER OFF.`

segments.voice: First, the corners. Leviticus 19 says: when you reap, don't reap the corner of your field all the way. That corner is called pe'ah, the edge. Second, what falls. Don't go back for the gleanings, the stalks that drop as you cut. In the vineyard, don't strip every last cluster, and don't pick up the fallen grapes. Then the reason, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God." Third, how big a corner? The Torah doesn't say. The Mishnah opens its tractate on the subject with a list of things that have no fixed measure, and pe'ah is first on the list, next to acts of kindness and Torah study. Then the rabbis set a floor: at least one sixtieth of the field. And a detail about dignity: the owner doesn't hand the corner out to people he likes. It's left standing, and those in need come and harvest it themselves. They aren't waiting on anyone's favor. Fourth, the story it made possible. Ruth, gleaning, ends up in the field of Boaz, a relative of her mother-in-law Naomi's late husband. He tells his workers to let some stalks fall on purpose for her. Their marriage, the Book of Ruth says, leads to King David. A line of kings, traced back to a field where the poor were allowed to gather.
screen: `PE'AH: THE EDGE LEFT STANDING.` · `GLEANINGS AND FALLEN GRAPES.` · `NO FIXED MEASURE.` · `RUTH IN THE FIELD OF BOAZ.` · then, large: `LEAVE THE CORNERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave something for someone else. Settle, and breathe. Think about the fields of your own life: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, your space. Where could you leave an edge uncut? Not a big donation. A corner. The last good parking spot. Part of a bonus. An hour of your week. Food you could leave at a pantry box, without needing to see who takes it. Pick one corner you'll leave this week. The bell holds the time.
Pe'ah. The corner of the field left unharvested, so the poor and the stranger can come and gather for themselves.
Your line: leave the corners. Today, leave one thing unclaimed on purpose, so someone else can take it without asking. Day four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Farmers in Israel who keep the agricultural laws still leave pe'ah, and some Jews outside farming see tzedakah, giving to those in need, as continuing the same commandment; the Mishnah's tractate Peah, which opens with the list of things without measure, is recited in the morning prayers.

myth: the Torah says exactly how big the corner must be
it doesn't. the Mishnah lists pe'ah first among things with no fixed measure; the rabbis set a minimum of one sixtieth.
the poor harvested the corner themselves
the owner doesn't choose who gets it. they come and gather.
Ruth's gleaning leads, in the story, to King David
she marries Boaz, and the Book of Ruth traces David from them.

fork.setup: you own the field. it's harvest, and a poor stranger is following your workers, picking up what drops. what does Leviticus 19 have you do?
options: send her away; the field is yours.
leave the corners and the fallen stalks for her.
fork.reveal: leave them for the poor and the stranger. Boaz went further: he had his workers drop stalks on purpose for Ruth.

original.note: Hebrew: edge, corner: the part of the field left for the poor (Leviticus 19:9).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old farming rule.
what it means: part of every harvest belongs, by right, to people in need, who gather it with dignity.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Peah 1:1 lists pe'ah among things without measure; 1:2 sets one sixtieth; Ruth 2 shows gleaning in practice.

sources.quoted: thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 19:10 'thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God.' quoted from memory; confirm.
Mishnah Peah 1:1 (things without measure) and 1:2 (pe'ah not less than one sixtieth); confirm.
Pe'ah given 'attached to the ground', the poor harvesting it themselves (Mishnah Peah 4:1–2): confirm.
Boaz tells his workers to pull out stalks for Ruth on purpose (Ruth 2:16); paraphrased.
Peah 1:1 is recited in the morning blessings in many prayer books (after the Torah blessings); confirm howItsDone wording.
Lev 23:22 repeats this law (day 418); that day takes the festival angle.

Editor review (y2 judaism 407–425): Boaz is a kinsman of Naomi's late husband (Ruth 2:1), not simply 'a relative of Naomi'; Ruth gleaned in the barley harvest first (Ruth 1:22, 2:23), so the hook's field is now barley; hook no longer opens 'Picture' or casts the listener as owner; the line of kings is now traced to a field open to gleaners rather than to 'a corner left uncut', since Ruth gleaned rather than took pe'ah; 'many Jews' softened in howItsDone.
